title: Stars — Birth, Life, and Death
description: How stars form, what powers them, and the endpoints of stellar evolution

concepts.title: Star Formation and the Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram
concepts.contentHtml:
Stars form when cold molecular gas clouds (mostly hydrogen) collapse under gravity. As the cloud collapses, it heats up — if the core reaches ~10 million K, hydrogen fusion ignites and a star is born.

The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram plots stellar luminosity (brightness) versus surface temperature. Most stars fall on the main sequence — a diagonal band from cool dim red stars to hot bright blue ones. Position on the main sequence is determined almost entirely by mass.

The Sun is a perfectly average middle-aged yellow dwarf, midway along the main sequence.

concepts.title: Nuclear Fusion — the Power Source of Stars
concepts.contentHtml:
Stars shine by nuclear fusion — fusing lighter nuclei into heavier ones, releasing energy via E = mc² (the mass of the products is slightly less than the reactants; the difference becomes energy).

In the Sun, the proton-proton chain fuses four hydrogen nuclei (protons) into one helium-4 nucleus: 4p → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν_e + energy. The mass deficit is ~0.7% of the original hydrogen mass — converted to ~3.8 × 10²⁶ watts.

Massive stars (>8 solar masses) also fuse helium into carbon, carbon into oxygen, and up through iron. Iron is the most stable nucleus — fusion beyond iron costs energy rather than releasing it.

concepts.title: Stellar Deaths — White Dwarfs, Neutron Stars, Black Holes
concepts.contentHtml:
How a star dies depends on its mass:

Low mass (< 8 M_Sun): Core becomes a white dwarf (electron-degenerate matter, Earth-sized, supported by electron degeneracy pressure). Outer layers puffed off as a planetary nebula.

Massive (8–20 M_Sun): Core collapses to a neutron star; outer layers explode in a supernova. The neutron star is city-sized but has density of an atomic nucleus — a teaspoon weighs ~100 million tonnes.

Very massive (>20 M_Sun): Core collapses directly to a black hole. Supernova may occur, or the star may 'quietly' implode.

title: Galaxies and the Large-Scale Structure
description: From the Milky Way to galaxy clusters and cosmic filaments

concepts.title: The Milky Way and Galaxy Types
concepts.contentHtml:
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy containing ~300 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. Our Sun sits about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre, in the Orion Arm.

Galaxies are classified by Hubble's tuning-fork diagram: spiral (like ours — flat discs with spiral arms, ongoing star formation), elliptical (old red stars, little gas, roughly spherical), and irregular (no clear shape — often the result of mergers).

Every large galaxy appears to have a supermassive black hole at its centre. The Milky Way's is Sagittarius A* — 4 million solar masses.

concepts.title: Dark Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
Galaxies rotate in a puzzling way: stars far from the centre orbit just as fast as stars near it — unlike planets in the Solar System (which orbit slower farther out, following Kepler's laws). This implies far more mass than we can see.

Fritz Zwicky first noticed this in galaxy clusters (1933). Vera Rubin's galaxy rotation curves (1970s) made it undeniable. The extra mass — dark matter — emits no light, interacts only gravitationally, and makes up ~27% of the universe's energy content.

Its nature is unknown. Leading candidates: WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles), axions, sterile neutrinos. No direct detection despite decades of experiments.

concepts.title: Cosmic Large-Scale Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
Galaxies are not randomly distributed. They cluster into groups and clusters (bound gravitationally), which string into filaments — and between the filaments are vast empty voids. This is the cosmic web.

The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years in diameter (larger than 13.8 billion light-years because space expanded while light was travelling). It contains ~2 trillion galaxies.

The large-scale structure reflects tiny quantum fluctuations in the early universe, magnified by gravity over 13.8 billion years — a direct link between quantum mechanics and cosmology.

title: Cosmology — The Big Bang and CMB
description: The origin, age, and early evolution of the universe

concepts.title: The Big Bang and Cosmic Timeline
concepts.contentHtml:
The universe began ~13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state. In the first second: fundamental particles formed. After ~3 minutes: protons and neutrons fused into light nuclei (Big Bang nucleosynthesis) — ~75% hydrogen, ~25% helium by mass.

After ~380,000 years: the universe cooled enough for electrons to combine with nuclei — atoms formed, making the universe transparent for the first time. The photons released at this moment travel to us today as the Cosmic Microwave Background.

After ~100–400 million years: the first stars formed, ending the 'cosmic dark ages'. The universe we observe today formed over the next 13 billion years.

concepts.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
concepts.contentHtml:
The CMB is thermal radiation from 380,000 years after the Big Bang, redshifted by the expansion of the universe from ~3000 K plasma temperature to ~2.725 K today. It arrives from all directions nearly uniformly.

Tiny temperature fluctuations (ΔT/T ~ 10⁻⁵) in the CMB map the density variations of the early universe that seeded all structure. The CMB power spectrum encodes cosmological parameters: the universe's age, composition, geometry, and the amplitude of primordial fluctuations.

Penzias and Wilson discovered the CMB accidentally in 1965 (Nobel 1978). COBE (1992), WMAP (2003), and Planck (2009–2018) mapped it in increasing detail.

concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.contentHtml:
The standard Big Bang model had problems: why is the CMB so uniform (horizon problem)? Why is space geometrically flat (flatness problem)? Why are there no magnetic monopoles?

Cosmic inflation (Guth 1981): in the first ~10⁻³⁶ to 10⁻³² seconds, the universe expanded exponentially — doubling in size ~60+ times. This smoothed out irregularities (solving the horizon and flatness problems) and diluted any monopoles.

Quantum fluctuations during inflation were stretched to cosmological scales, seeding the density variations seen in the CMB and the large-scale structure we observe today. Direct evidence for inflation (primordial gravitational waves in CMB polarisation — 'B-modes') is still being searched for.

title: Dark Energy and the Accelerating Universe
description: Why the universe's expansion is speeding up — and what drives it

concepts.title: The Discovery of Acceleration
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1998, two independent teams (led by Perlmutter, and by Schmidt and Riess) used Type Ia supernovae as 'standard candles' to measure cosmic distances. They found distant supernovae are dimmer than expected — the universe's expansion is not decelerating (as gravity should cause) but accelerating.

This was one of the most surprising discoveries in the history of cosmology. The Nobel Prize followed in 2011. Something — dubbed dark energy — must be driving the acceleration. Dark energy makes up ~68% of the universe's total energy content.

concepts.title: What is Dark Energy?
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest explanation: dark energy is the cosmological constant Λ — a constant energy density of empty space. In quantum field theory, vacuum fluctuations should contribute to this energy. But the predicted value is ~10¹²⁰ times larger than observed — the 'worst prediction in physics'.

Alternative: dark energy evolves over time (quintessence models). Or GR itself needs modification at cosmic scales. Or the acceleration is an artefact of inhomogeneity.

The cosmic inventory: ~68% dark energy, ~27% dark matter, ~5% ordinary matter (atoms). We understand only 5% of the universe's total content — the rest is unknown.

concepts.title: The Fate of the Universe
concepts.contentHtml:
The universe's fate depends on dark energy's nature:

Heat death (most likely with Λ = const): accelerating expansion continues forever. Galaxies outside the Local Group become unreachable. Stars die out. Black holes evaporate. Maximum entropy — cold, dark, empty.

Big Rip: if dark energy grows stronger over time (phantom energy), it eventually tears apart everything — galaxies, atoms, protons — in a finite time.

Big Crunch: if dark energy weakens, gravity eventually reverses expansion. The universe collapses back to a singularity.

Current data strongly favours heat death, but uncertainty in dark energy's equation of state keeps alternatives open.

title: Multi-Messenger Astronomy and Frontier Questions
description: Gravitational waves, neutrino astronomy, and the universe's deepest puzzles

concepts.title: Multi-Messenger Astronomy
concepts.contentHtml:
Until 2015, all astronomy was electromagnetic — looking at light (in all its forms). Now we can observe the universe through four 'messengers':

Light (EM): from radio to gamma rays — 400+ years of astronomy.
Gravitational waves: LIGO/Virgo, since 2015 — probe colliding compact objects.
Neutrinos: IceCube at South Pole detects high-energy neutrinos from cosmic accelerators; SN1987A was detected in neutrinos before optical light arrived.
Cosmic rays: ultra-high-energy particles (protons, nuclei) — Auger Observatory.

GW170817 (2017) was the first multi-messenger event: neutron star merger seen in GW + gamma rays + optical light simultaneously. It confirmed heavy element synthesis and constrained the speed of gravitational waves.

concepts.title: Exoplanets and the Search for Life
concepts.contentHtml:
As of 2025, over 5,600 confirmed exoplanets have been found. The Kepler and TESS missions use the transit method — measuring the tiny dip in starlight as a planet crosses in front of its star.

The habitable zone — where liquid water could exist on a rocky surface — hosts dozens of confirmed planets. Proxima Centauri b (4.2 light-years away) is in the habitable zone of the nearest star to the Sun.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is beginning to characterise exoplanet atmospheres via transmission spectroscopy. Detecting biosignatures (O₂, O₃, CH₄ out of equilibrium) would be the most profound discovery in human history.

concepts.title: Open Questions in Cosmology
concepts.contentHtml:
Astrophysics is entering a golden age — and facing its deepest puzzles:

— Hubble tension: local measurements of H₀ (~73 km/s/Mpc) disagree with CMB-inferred values (~67 km/s/Mpc) at 5σ — possibly hinting at new physics.
— Matter-antimatter asymmetry: the Big Bang produced equal amounts, but the universe is made of matter. Why? CP violation in the Standard Model is insufficient.
— Before the Big Bang: classical GR breaks down at t = 0. Quantum gravity might reveal a bounce, a multiverse, or something entirely new.
— Dark matter identity: despite decades of search, no WIMP has been detected directly.

The next generation of telescopes (LISA, ELT, SKA, Rubin Observatory) will tackle these questions over the coming decades.

title: Stellar Evolution
description: From cloud to corpse — a star's life story

concepts.title: From Molecular Cloud to Main Sequence
concepts.contentHtml:
Star formation begins in cold, dense molecular clouds (~10 K, ~10⁴ molecules/cm³). Gravity overcomes pressure when the Jeans mass is exceeded, and the cloud collapses.

Collapse heats the core; eventually it ignites hydrogen fusion, and the star reaches the main sequence — stable for a long time as gravity balances thermal pressure.

The main-sequence lifetime is approximately 10 billion years × (M/M_sun)^(-2.5). The Sun has 5 billion years left; a 10-solar-mass star lives only ~30 million years before exhausting its fuel.

concepts.title: Red Giants & Helium Burning
concepts.contentHtml:
When core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and heats further while the outer envelope expands and cools — the star becomes a red giant.

If the core gets hot enough (~10⁸ K), helium fusion starts via the triple-alpha process: 3 He-4 → C-12. This is the only way nature creates carbon, and the precise nuclear physics of this reaction is one reason the universe contains carbon-based life.

For solar-mass stars, the journey ends after helium burning. Heavier stars continue: carbon burning, neon, oxygen, silicon — making heavier elements all the way to iron.

concepts.title: End States
concepts.contentHtml:
Stars end their lives in different ways depending on initial mass:

• Solar-mass (M < 8 M_sun): planetary nebula + white dwarf core (~Earth-size, electron-degeneracy supported).
• Massive (8 < M < 25 M_sun): core-collapse supernova → neutron star (~20 km, neutron degenerate).
• Very massive (M > 25 M_sun): supernova → stellar-mass black hole.

The mass distribution of compact remnants is a fingerprint of late-stage stellar physics.

title: Compact Objects
description: White dwarfs, neutron stars, and exotic interiors

concepts.title: White Dwarfs and the Chandrasekhar Limit
concepts.contentHtml:
A white dwarf is the carbon/oxygen core of a low-mass star, supported by electron degeneracy pressure (a quantum effect — Pauli exclusion).

Subramanyan Chandrasekhar showed (Nobel 1983) that no white dwarf can exceed about 1.4 solar masses. Above this Chandrasekhar limit, electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support the star against gravity.

Type Ia supernovae are the explosion of a white dwarf pushed over the limit by mass accretion. Their standardizable luminosity makes them the cosmic distance ladder's top rung.

concepts.title: Neutron Stars
concepts.contentHtml:
A neutron star packs ~1.4 solar masses into a 20-km sphere — density of an atomic nucleus, magnetic fields up to 10¹⁵ G, and surface gravity 10¹¹ times Earth's.

Some neutron stars are pulsars: rotating beams of radio (or X-ray, or gamma) emission seen as periodic pulses. The fastest known spin at over 700 Hz; Hulse and Taylor's binary pulsar (Nobel 1993) provided the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves.

The interior may be exotic: superfluid neutrons, superconducting protons, possibly quark matter at the center. The neutron-star equation of state is hot research, constrained by GW170817's tidal deformability measurement.

concepts.title: Black Holes & Their Diet
concepts.contentHtml:
Above ~3 solar masses (Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit), even neutron degeneracy fails. The result is a black hole.

Stellar-mass black holes are remnants of massive stars. Supermassive black holes (10⁶-10¹⁰ solar masses) lurk at galaxy centers; how they grew so big so fast in the early universe is unclear.

Accreting black holes are some of the brightest objects in the universe — quasars and active galactic nuclei. Friction in the accretion disk converts up to 40% of rest-mass energy to radiation, dwarfing fusion's ~0.7%.

title: Galaxies & Large-Scale Structure
description: How matter is arranged on the largest scales

concepts.title: Galaxy Types
concepts.contentHtml:
Galaxies fall mainly into spirals (like the Milky Way and Andromeda), ellipticals (mostly old stars, gas-poor, often the result of mergers), and irregulars.

The Hubble sequence categorizes them by morphology. Modern observations show galaxy types correlate with environment — clusters are dominated by ellipticals, while spirals live mostly in the field.

Galactic morphology, star formation history, and chemical abundances tell a layered story of cosmic evolution.

concepts.title: The Cosmic Web
concepts.contentHtml:
Galaxies are not distributed randomly. They cluster on filaments and sheets, surrounding vast voids — the cosmic web.

This structure emerged from tiny density fluctuations in the early universe, growing under gravity. Dark matter is the scaffolding; baryons fall into its potential wells, where galaxies form.

Large surveys (SDSS, DESI) map this cosmic web across hundreds of millions of light-years, providing crisp tests of cosmological models.

concepts.title: Galactic Dynamics & Dark Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
Stars in galactic disks rotate at roughly constant speed independent of distance from the center — flat rotation curves. Visible matter alone predicts Keplerian fall-off (v ∝ r^(-1/2)).

Vera Rubin's 1970s observations of flat rotation curves, plus later observations of galaxy cluster dynamics, gravitational lensing, and the CMB, demand that ~85% of all matter in the universe is dark matter.

What dark matter is remains unknown. WIMPs, axions, primordial black holes, and modified gravity are all candidate explanations — none yet confirmed.
